using Random, Statistics

const VALUES = Dict('T' => 3.0, 'R' => 8.0, 'D' => 12.0)    # topaz < ruby < diamond
const COMPOSITION = ['T', 'T', 'T', 'R', 'D']
const REVEAL = Dict(:none => nothing, :low => 'T', :medium => 'R', :high => 'D')

struct View
    stage::Int
    rival::Bool
    revealed::Dict{Int,Char}
    counts::Vector{Int}
end

function ev_unknown(v::View)
    hidden = copy(COMPOSITION)
    for g in values(v.revealed)
        deleteat!(hidden, findfirst(==(g), hidden))
    end
    isempty(hidden) ? 0.0 : mean(VALUES[g] for g in hidden)
end

function utilities(v::View; bonus = 0.5)
    mu = ev_unknown(v)
    map(eachindex(v.counts)) do j
        known = haskey(v.revealed, j)
        base = known ? VALUES[v.revealed[j]] : mu
        v.rival && (base /= v.counts[j] + 1)
        fresh = !known && v.counts[j] == 0
        base + (v.stage == 1 && fresh ? bonus : 0.0)
    end
end

logit_agent(tau; bonus = 0.5) = (rng, v) -> begin
    u = utilities(v; bonus)
    tau == 0 && return rand(rng, findall(x -> isapprox(x, maximum(u)), u))
    w = exp.((u .- maximum(u)) ./ tau)
    c = cumsum(w ./ sum(w))
    min(searchsortedfirst(c, rand(rng)), length(u))
end

function explorer_agent(rng, v)
    for (j, g) in v.revealed
        g == 'D' && return j
    end
    unknown = [j for j in eachindex(v.counts) if !haskey(v.revealed, j)]
    fresh = [j for j in unknown if v.counts[j] == 0]
    rand(rng, isempty(fresh) ? unknown : fresh)
end

function play_round(rng, agents, condition; rival = false)
    m, n = length(COMPOSITION), length(agents)
    gems = shuffle(rng, COMPOSITION)
    revealed = Dict{Int,Char}()
    if REVEAL[condition] !== nothing
        j = rand(rng, findall(==(REVEAL[condition]), gems))
        revealed[j] = gems[j]
    end
    payoff, explored, found = zeros(n), falses(n), false
    for stage in 1:2
        counts, picks = zeros(Int, m), zeros(Int, n)
        for i in randperm(rng, n)                       # random sequential order
            picks[i] = agents[i](rng, View(stage, rival, copy(revealed), copy(counts)))
            counts[picks[i]] += 1
            stage == 1 && (explored[i] = !haskey(revealed, picks[i]))
        end
        for (i, j) in enumerate(picks)
            payoff[i] += VALUES[gems[j]] / (rival ? counts[j] : 1)
            found |= gems[j] == 'D'
        end
        foreach(j -> (revealed[j] = gems[j]), picks)     # stage-1 finds become public
    end
    payoff, found, explored
end

function simulate(agents, condition; rounds = 500, rival = false, seed = 0)
    rng = MersenneTwister(seed)
    out = [play_round(rng, agents, condition; rival) for _ in 1:rounds]
    share = mean(sum(o[1]) for o in out) / (2 * length(agents) * VALUES['D'])
    share, mean(o[2] for o in out), mean(o[3] for o in out)
end

rational = fill(logit_agent(0.0), 5)
for c in (:none, :low, :medium, :high)
    s, b, _ = simulate(rational, c; rounds = 600)
    sr, br, _ = simulate(rational, c; rounds = 600, rival = true)
    println(rpad(string(c), 8), " share ", round(s, digits = 2), " brk ", round(b, digits = 2),
            " | rival share ", round(sr, digits = 2), " brk ", round(br, digits = 2))
end
for tau in (0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2)
    _, b, _ = simulate(fill(logit_agent(tau), 5), :medium; rounds = 400, seed = 1)
    println("tau = ", tau, "  breakthrough with ruby revealed = ", round(b, digits = 2))
end
// Cargo.toml: rand = "0.8"
use rand::rngs::StdRng;
use rand::seq::SliceRandom;
use rand::{Rng, SeedableRng};
use std::collections::HashMap;

const COMPOSITION: [char; 5] = ['T', 'T', 'T', 'R', 'D'];

fn value(g: char) -> f64 {
    match g { 'T' => 3.0, 'R' => 8.0, _ => 12.0 } // topaz < ruby < diamond
}

struct View { stage: u8, rival: bool, revealed: HashMap<usize, char>, counts: Vec<usize> }

type Agent = Box<dyn Fn(&mut StdRng, &View) -> usize>;

fn ev_unknown(v: &View) -> f64 {
    let mut hidden = COMPOSITION.to_vec();
    for g in v.revealed.values() {
        let k = hidden.iter().position(|h| h == g).unwrap();
        hidden.remove(k);
    }
    if hidden.is_empty() { 0.0 } else { hidden.iter().map(|&g| value(g)).sum::<f64>() / hidden.len() as f64 }
}

fn utilities(v: &View, bonus: f64) -> Vec<f64> {
    let mu = ev_unknown(v);
    (0..v.counts.len()).map(|j| {
        let known = v.revealed.contains_key(&j);
        let mut base = if known { value(v.revealed[&j]) } else { mu };
        if v.rival { base /= (v.counts[j] + 1) as f64; }
        let fresh = !known && v.counts[j] == 0;
        base + if v.stage == 1 && fresh { bonus } else { 0.0 }
    }).collect()
}

fn logit_agent(tau: f64) -> Agent {
    Box::new(move |rng, v| {
        let u = utilities(v, 0.5);
        let umax = u.iter().cloned().fold(f64::MIN, f64::max);
        if tau == 0.0 {
            let best: Vec<usize> = (0..u.len()).filter(|&j| (u[j] - umax).abs() < 1e-9).collect();
            return *best.choose(rng).unwrap();
        }
        let w: Vec<f64> = u.iter().map(|x| ((x - umax) / tau).exp()).collect();
        let mut r = rng.gen::<f64>() * w.iter().sum::<f64>();
        for (j, wj) in w.iter().enumerate() {
            if r < *wj { return j; }
            r -= wj;
        }
        u.len() - 1
    })
}

fn play_round(rng: &mut StdRng, agents: &[Agent], reveal: Option<char>, rival: bool) -> (f64, bool) {
    let (m, n) = (COMPOSITION.len(), agents.len());
    let mut gems = COMPOSITION.to_vec();
    gems.shuffle(rng);
    let mut revealed: HashMap<usize, char> = HashMap::new();
    if let Some(target) = reveal {
        let idx: Vec<usize> = (0..m).filter(|&j| gems[j] == target).collect();
        let j = *idx.choose(rng).unwrap();
        revealed.insert(j, gems[j]);
    }
    let (mut total, mut found) = (0.0, false);
    for stage in 1..=2u8 {
        let mut counts = vec![0usize; m];
        let mut picks = vec![0usize; n];
        let mut order: Vec<usize> = (0..n).collect();
        order.shuffle(rng); // random sequential order
        for i in order {
            let view = View { stage, rival, revealed: revealed.clone(), counts: counts.clone() };
            picks[i] = agents[i](rng, &view);
            counts[picks[i]] += 1;
        }
        for &j in &picks {
            total += value(gems[j]) / if rival { counts[j] as f64 } else { 1.0 };
            found |= gems[j] == 'D';
        }
        for &j in &picks { revealed.insert(j, gems[j]); } // stage-1 finds become public
    }
    (total, found)
}

fn simulate(agents: &[Agent], reveal: Option<char>, rounds: usize, rival: bool, seed: u64) -> (f64, f64) {
    let mut rng = StdRng::seed_from_u64(seed);
    let (mut share, mut brk) = (0.0, 0.0);
    for _ in 0..rounds {
        let (t, d) = play_round(&mut rng, agents, reveal, rival);
        share += t / (2.0 * agents.len() as f64 * 12.0);
        brk += d as u8 as f64;
    }
    (share / rounds as f64, brk / rounds as f64)
}

fn main() {
    let rational: Vec<Agent> = (0..5).map(|_| logit_agent(0.0)).collect();
    for (name, reveal) in [("none", None), ("low", Some('T')), ("medium", Some('R')), ("high", Some('D'))] {
        let (s, b) = simulate(&rational, reveal, 600, false, 0);
        let (sr, br) = simulate(&rational, reveal, 600, true, 0);
        println!("{:<8} share {:.2} brk {:.2} | rival share {:.2} brk {:.2}", name, s, b, sr, br);
    }
    for tau in [0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2] {
        let agents: Vec<Agent> = (0..5).map(|_| logit_agent(tau)).collect();
        let (_, b) = simulate(&agents, Some('R'), 400, false, 1);
        println!("tau {:.1}: breakthrough with ruby revealed {:.2}", tau, b);
    }
}

The baseline reproduces three of the paper’s findings from payoffs alone: the herd, the rivalry reversal, and, through \(\tau\), the gap between machines and people. It does not reproduce the fourth. In Figure 227.11 (c), adding explorers lifts the breakthrough rate to one with just two of them, but the unprimed best responders keep sitting on the ruby, because under non-rival payoffs someone else’s exploration does not change the private value of exploring; it only makes free riding more attractive. That the LLM agents did explore more is therefore either a disposition the mechanistic model leaves out (conformity to a group norm, or an implicit sense of a shared goal) or an artifact of how the model reads its prompt. This is the division of labor the paper proposes: the LLM agents surface a surprise, a transparent model shows it does not follow from incentives alone, and only an experiment with people can say whether people do it.

Swapping in a language model. Because the engine passes each agent a public view and receives an index, replacing a rule with a model changes one function. The sketch below, not executed here, drives the same engine with any OpenAI-compatible server, for example a local Ollama or vLLM instance hosting an open-weight model, and logs each rationale so it can be read and coded afterwards.

# Show-only: an LLM-backed agent for the engine above (needs a running model server).
import re
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")
NAMES = {"T": "topaz ($3)", "R": "ruby ($8)", "D": "diamond ($12)"}


def rules(view):
    split = ("Players who choose the same mountain split its value equally." if view["rival"]
             else "Players who choose the same mountain each receive its full value.")
    return ("There are 5 mountains hiding three topazes ($3 each), one ruby ($8) and one "
            "diamond ($12). In each of two stages you choose one mountain and earn the value "
            f"of its gem. {split} Gems found in stage 1 are revealed to everyone before "
            "stage 2. Your objective is to maximize your own earnings.")


def llm_agent(model="qwen3:8b", persona="", temperature=1.0, log=None):
    def choose(rng, view):
        known = "; ".join(f"Mountain {j + 1} holds a {NAMES[g]}"
                          for j, g in sorted(view["revealed"].items())) or "nothing"
        taken = ", ".join(f"Mountain {j + 1}: {c}"
                          for j, c in enumerate(view["counts"]) if c) or "none yet"
        prompt = (f"{rules(view)} {persona}\nStage {view['stage']}. Known: {known}. "
                  f"Players who already chose this stage: {taken}.\n"
                  "Answer 'Mountain k' on the first line, then one sentence explaining why.")
        reply = client.chat.completions.create(
            model=model, temperature=temperature,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]).choices[0].message.content
        hit = re.search(r"Mountain\s*(\d+)", reply)
        valid = hit is not None and 1 <= int(hit.group(1)) <= view["m"]
        j = int(hit.group(1)) - 1 if valid else int(rng.integers(view["m"]))
        if log is not None:
            log.append({"stage": view["stage"], "choice": j, "parsed": valid, "reply": reply})
        return j
    return choose

# risk_lover = "You are a risk-loving person who enjoys gambling on high rewards."

Using the method responsibly. The paper’s own guidance, which applies to any LLM simulation in economics, comes down to five practices. First, replicate a known human result before extrapolating; the human data act as a holdout set, and without one there is no basis for trusting the untested conditions. Second, run manipulation checks, as with the risk-preference task, so that a prompt that says “risk-loving” is shown to change risk attitudes. Third, treat rationales as hypotheses: the agents explained herding as conformity, but a rationale can be a post hoc justification, so the authors lean on its consistency with the choices actually made, with the human patterns, and with the step-by-step traces of reasoning models, never on the rationale alone. Fourth, report the model and version, the prompt templates, the sampling settings, and the number of runs, because results can move with any of them. Fifth, remember what the model cannot represent: its training text over-represents English-speaking, urban, digitally visible populations, a bias that, unlike a WEIRD subject pool, cannot be fixed by recruiting differently, and it shows framing and anchoring effects of its own.

Set beside Ashokkumar et al. (2026), the paper sharpens where simulation earns its keep. Simulated respondents predicted survey treatment effects well because each effect is a property of individual responses. In the streetlight game, asking GPT-4 to predict the outcome did poorly, while letting GPT-4 agents play it reproduced the result, because the outcome is a property of the interaction. When the quantity of interest is an equilibrium, the interaction has to be simulated, not described. The economic consequence is the one Section 227.1.5 anticipates. A two-order-of-magnitude fall in the cost of a pilot changes which experiments get designed and which boundary conditions get checked before money is spent on human subjects, while the judgment about which of the machine’s surprises are worth testing stays with the researcher.

227.18 Platform Power and Algorithmic Markets

227.18.1 The Algorithmic Marketplace

Platform economics in the AI age represents a fundamental shift in how markets operate. Fletcher and colleagues demonstrate how recommender systems shape supplier competition on platforms, showing that ranking algorithms can tilt competition in ways that are difficult for regulators to detect or remedy. Their analysis reveals that platforms can extract monopoly rents while maintaining the appearance of competition, as suppliers compete fiercely for algorithmic favor rather than consumer preference.

Calvano and colleagues model how AI recommender systems affect market concentration and consumer surplus. They find that even well-intentioned algorithms designed to maximize user satisfaction can lead to market concentration and reduced innovation. The mechanism is subtle: by learning to recommend products that users are likely to purchase, algorithms inadvertently favor established products with proven track records over innovative newcomers. This creates barriers to entry that are particularly challenging because they emerge from seemingly neutral technological systems rather than deliberate anti-competitive behavior.

227.18.1.1 Pricing Algorithms and Digital Collusion

Brown and MacKay demonstrate that simple pricing algorithms can increase price levels and facilitate tacit collusion without explicit communication between competitors. When multiple firms use similar pricing algorithms that learn from market conditions, they can converge on supra-competitive prices that would be difficult to sustain with human decision-making. This algorithmic collusion is particularly concerning because it may not violate existing antitrust laws, which typically require evidence of explicit agreement between competitors.

Clark and colleagues review recent cases where pricing algorithms may enable collusion, including investigations into algorithmic pricing in rental housing markets. The U.S. Department of Justice’s increasing focus on algorithmic collusion represents a new frontier in antitrust enforcement. Traditional tools for detecting and prosecuting collusion, looking for communications between competitors, identifying explicit agreements, become ineffective when collusion emerges from algorithmic learning rather than human conspiracy.

The challenge for regulators is profound. Algorithms can achieve collusive outcomes through trial and error learning without being programmed to collude. They can respond to competitor actions in microseconds, enabling forms of signaling and coordination that would be impossible for human managers. They can also provide plausible deniability, as firms can claim they didn’t intend anti-competitive outcomes that emerged from complex machine learning systems they don’t fully understand.

227.18.1.2 Platform AI and Market Power

Recent empirical studies on ride-sharing platforms’ dynamic pricing and hotel pricing algorithms provide concrete examples of how platform AI affects prices and consumer welfare. These systems optimize complex objective functions that balance multiple stakeholder interests, consumers, suppliers, and the platform itself. While they can increase efficiency by better matching supply and demand, they also enable sophisticated forms of price discrimination and can extract consumer surplus in ways that would be impossible without AI.

The concentration of AI capabilities among major platforms creates new forms of market power. Platforms with superior AI systems can offer better user experiences, attracting more users and generating more data to further improve their AI. This creates winner-take-all dynamics that are difficult to disrupt through traditional competition. Startups may have innovative ideas but lack the data and computational resources to compete with incumbent platforms’ AI capabilities.

227.18.1.3 AI Summaries and the Review Commons

Platforms no longer only rank and price; they also write. The most visible example is the AI-generated review summary, a short paragraph at the top of a product page that condenses hundreds of customer reviews into a few lines about what buyers like and dislike. The summary is made entirely of user-generated content, so its long-run value depends on whether customers keep writing reviews, and a standard public-goods argument predicts that they will not. A review is a voluntary contribution to a shared stock of product knowledge, its payoff to the writer is mostly the sense of helping other shoppers, and if shoppers read the summary instead of the reviews, each new review reaches fewer readers. On that logic the summary crowds out the contributions it is built from. The worry is not hypothetical. In a study of programming questions and answers, Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva, and Wachs (2024) find that within six months of ChatGPT’s release, activity on Stack Overflow fell by 25% relative to its Russian and Chinese counterparts, where access to ChatGPT was limited, and to similar mathematics forums, where ChatGPT was less capable; the decline hit the public archive that future models need for training.

Wang et al. (2026) examine what happened to consumer reviews when AI-generated summaries were introduced in e-commerce and find the opposite of crowd-out: review volume went up. Their explanation is collective efficacy, the belief that one’s own input meaningfully contributes to a shared body of product knowledge. By presenting the reviews as one aggregated voice, the summary makes the collective visible and shows each prospective reviewer that the crowd’s input is actually used. A controlled laboratory experiment supports the mechanism: the authors measure perceived collective efficacy directly and find that it mediates the effect of the summary on the likelihood of leaving a review. Two moderation results sharpen the picture: the increase is larger for well-reviewed products than for under-reviewed ones, and larger for polarizing products than for non-polarizing ones. The reviews themselves also change. After the summaries appear, reviews are richer in content and complement the summary rather than duplicate it: contributors discuss fewer of the product attributes the summary already covers, discuss more of the attributes it leaves out, and when they do address a summarized attribute they elaborate on it instead of restating it.

A two-channel model. The conflict between the crowd-out prediction and the evidence is easiest to see in a model with two channels. A prospective reviewer \(i\) writes a review if its perceived benefit exceeds a private cost \(c_i\), drawn independently from a continuous distribution \(F\) on the positive reals. Write the benefit as the product of two terms: \(v\), the informational value of a review to other shoppers, and \(e\), the reviewer’s perceived efficacy, the probability that the review actually shapes what the collective knows. The review rate is

\[ r = \Pr(c_i < e\,v) = F(e\,v). \tag{227.8}\]

A summary acts on both terms. Crowd-out lowers the informational value, \(v \mapsto (1-s)\,v\), where \(s \in [0,1)\) is the share of reader attention the summary diverts from individual reviews. Collective efficacy raises perceived efficacy, \(e \mapsto (1+\kappa)\,e\), with \(\kappa \ge 0\). Because \(F\) is strictly increasing, the review rate rises exactly when the benefit index rises:

\[ \begin{aligned} r_{\text{after}} > r_{\text{before}} &\iff F\big((1+\kappa)(1-s)\,e\,v\big) > F(e\,v) \\ &\iff (1+\kappa)(1-s) > 1 \\ &\iff \kappa > \frac{1}{1-s} - 1 = \frac{s}{1-s} \equiv \kappa^*(s). \end{aligned} \tag{227.9}\]

Two features of Equation 227.9 matter. First, the sign of the volume effect does not depend on the cost distribution \(F\), only on the strengths of the two channels. A finding that volume rose is therefore a statement that the efficacy gain outran the crowd-out loss, whatever the distribution of reviewers’ effort costs; \(F\) governs only the magnitude. Second, the break-even efficacy gain is convex in the crowd-out share, since \(d^2\kappa^*/ds^2 = 2/(1-s)^3 > 0\). A summary that diverts 20% of reader attention needs a 25% efficacy gain to break even, but one that diverts 50% needs a 100% gain. As summaries get better at answering shoppers’ questions, the efficacy channel has to work harder to keep the commons growing, which is a reason to read the published result as a property of current summary designs rather than a permanent law.

The moderation results read naturally as statements about where \(\kappa\) is large. A summary of a well-reviewed product visibly rests on many voices, which plausibly makes the collective more salient than a summary assembled from a handful of reviews. On a polarizing product the summary has to balance conflicting views, so a prospective reviewer can more easily imagine one more review shifting what it says. This reading is ours rather than a result the paper derives, but it is consistent with the efficacy mechanism the laboratory experiment measures.

Where reviewers spend their words. The content results have a parallel logic. Index product attributes by \(j = 1, \dots, K\), each with a salience \(w_j\), how likely a buyer is to notice the attribute and want to discuss it, and a corpus coverage \(q_j \in [0,1]\), how thoroughly existing reviews already discuss it. Suppose a reviewer mentions attribute \(j\) with probability proportional to its salience, discounted by how little the mention would add:

\[ m_j = \frac{w_j\,(1-\hat q_j)^{\gamma}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\,(1-\hat q_k)^{\gamma}}, \tag{227.10}\]

where \(\hat q_j\) is the reviewer’s perceived coverage and \(\gamma > 0\) measures how much the reviewer cares about adding something new. Without a summary, few buyers read hundreds of reviews before writing their own, so perceived coverage is flat, \(\hat q_j = \bar q\) for every \(j\); the discount then cancels from Equation 227.10 and mentions are proportional to salience, so reviewers restate what everyone notices. A summary makes coverage visible, \(\hat q_j = q_j\). Because the most salient attributes are also the best covered, mentions shift toward the attributes the corpus has neglected, and the expected new information in a review, \(I = \sum_j m_j\,(1 - q_j)\), rises.

The simulation below puts numbers on both channels, with a SymPy check of the threshold in Equation 227.9. Reviewer costs are exponential, so \(F(x) = 1 - e^{-x}\), the baseline review rate is about 26%, and the summary covers the four best-covered of twelve attributes. It is a stylized illustration of the mechanism with parameters chosen for exposition, not an estimate from the study’s data.

  • Python
  • Julia
  • Rust
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm
import pandas as pd
import sympy as sp

# Volume channel: write iff c_i < e * v, so the review rate is F(e * v).
# The summary maps v -> (1 - s) v (crowd-out) and e -> (1 + kappa) e (efficacy).
s_sym, k_sym = sp.symbols("s kappa", positive=True)
kappa_star = sp.solve(sp.Eq((1 + k_sym) * (1 - s_sym), 1), k_sym)[0]
print("kappa* == s / (1 - s):", sp.simplify(kappa_star - s_sym / (1 - s_sym)) == 0)
print("d2 kappa*/ds2 == 2 / (1 - s)^3:", sp.simplify(sp.diff(kappa_star, s_sym, 2) - 2 / (1 - s_sym) ** 3) == 0)

lam, e0, v0 = 1.0, 0.30, 1.0          # exponential costs: baseline review rate about 26%

def review_rate(e, v):
    return 1.0 - np.exp(-lam * e * v)

s_grid = np.linspace(0.0, 0.6, 121)
k_grid = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 101)
S, KAP = np.meshgrid(s_grid, k_grid)
pct_change = 100 * (review_rate(e0 * (1 + KAP), v0 * (1 - S)) / review_rate(e0, v0) - 1)

# Content channel: mentions proportional to w_j (1 - q_hat_j)^gamma.
K, gamma = 12, 2.0
w = 1.0 / np.arange(1, K + 1) ** 0.8          # salience, Zipf-like
w /= w.sum()
q = 0.85 * w / w.max()                         # coverage tracks salience
covered = np.arange(K) < 4                     # the summary covers the 4 best-covered attributes

def mention_shares(q_hat):
    m = w * (1 - q_hat) ** gamma
    return m / m.sum()

m_before = mention_shares(np.full(K, q.mean()))   # coverage invisible before the summary
m_after = mention_shares(q)                       # the summary makes coverage visible

def info(m):
    return float(np.sum(m * (1 - q)))

s_ex, k_ex = 0.30, 0.60

r1 = review_rate(e0 * (1 + k_ex), v0 * (1 - s_ex))

)

using Statistics, Printf

# Volume channel: the review rate is F(e v); the summary maps v -> (1 - s) v and e -> (1 + kappa) e
kappa_star(s) = s / (1 - s)
review_rate(e, v; lam = 1.0) = 1 - exp(-lam * e * v)

e0, v0, s, kappa = 0.30, 1.0, 0.30, 0.60
r0 = review_rate(e0, v0)
r1 = review_rate(e0 * (1 + kappa), v0 * (1 - s))
@printf("kappa* at s = %.2f: %.3f\n", s, kappa_star(s))
@printf("review rate: %.3f -> %.3f (%+.1f%%)\n", r0, r1, 100 * (r1 / r0 - 1))

# Content channel: mentions proportional to w_j (1 - qhat_j)^gamma
K, gamma = 12, 2.0
w = 1 ./ (1:K) .^ 0.8
w ./= sum(w)
q = 0.85 .* w ./ maximum(w)
covered = (1:K) .<= 4

shares(qhat) = (m = w .* (1 .- qhat) .^ gamma; m ./ sum(m))
info(m) = sum(m .* (1 .- q))

m_before = shares(fill(mean(q), K))   # coverage invisible before the summary
m_after = shares(q)                   # the summary makes coverage visible
for (name, m, r) in (("before", m_before, r0), ("after", m_after, r1))
    @printf("%-6s  summarized share %.3f  other share %.3f  info/review %.3f  info/buyer %.3f\n",
            name, sum(m[covered]), sum(m[.!covered]), info(m), r * info(m))
end
// Volume channel: the review rate is F(e v) with exponential costs, F(x) = 1 - exp(-x)
fn review_rate(e: f64, v: f64) -> f64 {
    1.0 - (-e * v).exp()
}

// Content channel: mentions proportional to w_j (1 - qhat_j)^gamma, normalised to shares
fn shares(w: &[f64], qhat: &[f64], gamma: f64) -> Vec<f64> {
    let m: Vec<f64> = w.iter().zip(qhat).map(|(wj, qj)| wj * (1.0 - qj).powf(gamma)).collect();
    let total: f64 = m.iter().sum();
    m.iter().map(|x| x / total).collect()
}

fn info(m: &[f64], q: &[f64]) -> f64 {
    m.iter().zip(q).map(|(mj, qj)| mj * (1.0 - qj)).sum()
}

fn main() {
    let (e0, v0, s, kappa) = (0.30, 1.0, 0.30, 0.60);
    let r0 = review_rate(e0, v0);
    let r1 = review_rate(e0 * (1.0 + kappa), v0 * (1.0 - s));
    println!("kappa* at s = {s:.2}: {:.3}", s / (1.0 - s));
    println!("review rate: {r0:.3} -> {r1:.3} ({:+.1}%)", 100.0 * (r1 / r0 - 1.0));

    let (k, gamma) = (12usize, 2.0);
    let raw: Vec<f64> = (1..=k).map(|j| 1.0 / (j as f64).powf(0.8)).collect();
    let total: f64 = raw.iter().sum();
    let w: Vec<f64> = raw.iter().map(|x| x / total).collect();
    let w_max = w.iter().cloned().fold(f64::MIN, f64::max);
    let q: Vec<f64> = w.iter().map(|x| 0.85 * x / w_max).collect();
    let q_bar = q.iter().sum::<f64>() / k as f64;

    let before = shares(&w, &vec![q_bar; k], gamma); // coverage invisible before the summary
    let after = shares(&w, &q, gamma); // the summary makes coverage visible
    for (name, m, r) in [("before", &before, r0), ("after", &after, r1)] {
        let summarized: f64 = m[..4].iter().sum();
        println!(
            "{name:<6}  summarized share {summarized:.3}  other share {:.3}  info/review {:.3}  info/buyer {:.3}",
            1.0 - summarized,
            info(m, &q),
            r * info(m, &q)
        );
    }
}

In the worked example the summary diverts 30% of reader attention, which by Equation 227.9 requires an efficacy gain above \(\kappa^* = 0.43\); with \(\kappa = 0.6\) the review rate rises by about 10%, and the left panel of Figure 227.12 shows how quickly that margin disappears as \(s\) grows. The content channel is larger. Once coverage is visible, the share of mentions going to the four summarized attributes falls from 60% to 33%, the eight neglected attributes go from 40% to 67%, and the new information carried by an average review rises by about 32%. The two gains compound: more buyers write and each review adds more, so the new information produced per buyer rises by about 45% (\(1.10 \times 1.32\)). The most heavily covered attribute is the clearest case: before the summary it drew about a quarter of all mentions, afterwards about 1%, which is the model’s version of the paper’s finding that contributors stop restating what the summary already says.

For platform design the result recasts the summary from a substitute for the review commons into a coordination device for it. A summary that shows contributors what is already known, and by omission what is not, directs their effort toward the gaps. That is the reverse of the homogenization dynamic in Section 227.1.6, where individuals drawing from the same model converge on the statistical center, and the difference lies in how the model’s output is used. When the generated text stands in for each person’s own contribution, diversity falls; when it serves as a map of what has already been contributed, contributors spread out. Equation 227.9 also says how the result could fail. A summary that answers so many questions that shoppers rarely scroll past it raises \(s\), and unless the page also signals that reviews still matter, for instance by visibly tying the summary to the reviews it condenses or by inviting comment on the attributes it leaves out, the crowd-out channel will eventually dominate.

227.19 The Entrepreneurial AI Revolution

227.19.1 AI as Entrepreneurial Enabler

The impact of AI on entrepreneurship and small business represents one of the most democratizing yet disruptive forces in the modern economy. Giuggioli and Pellegrini provide a systematic review showing how AI fundamentally changes opportunity recognition, business model design, and scaling dynamics for entrepreneurs. AI lowers barriers to entry by providing small firms access to capabilities previously available only to large corporations, sophisticated market analysis, personalized customer engagement, automated operations management.

Fossen and colleagues survey emerging empirical work documenting AI’s multifaceted effects on entrepreneurship. New ventures using AI show 40% higher survival rates in their first three years compared to traditional startups. The mechanisms are diverse: AI helps entrepreneurs validate ideas faster through rapid market testing, optimize resource allocation with predictive analytics, and scale operations without proportional increases in headcount. However, the benefits are unevenly distributed. Entrepreneurs with technical backgrounds capture most gains, while those without AI literacy struggle to compete.

227.19.1.1 The Productivity Paradox for Startups

Heller and colleagues analyze startup funding dynamics, showing that software startups exposed to tools like GitHub Copilot raise funds faster while maintaining smaller development teams. A typical AI-augmented startup can achieve the development velocity of a traditional team three times its size. This has profound implications for venture capital: investors now expect startups to achieve more with less, raising the bar for what constitutes fundable traction.

Uriarte and colleagues map how AI reshapes core entrepreneurial processes. In opportunity recognition, AI analyzes vast datasets to identify unmet needs and market gaps that human entrepreneurs might miss. In business model design, AI enables new forms of value creation, from AI-generated content businesses to algorithmic matching platforms. In scaling, AI allows startups to serve global markets from day one, without the traditional constraints of human resources or physical infrastructure.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s 2024 study documents rapid but uneven AI adoption among small and medium enterprises (SMEs). While 68% of SMEs report experimenting with AI tools, only 23% have integrated AI into core business processes. The main barriers are not technological but organizational: lack of AI literacy (42%), uncertainty about ROI (38%), and fear of dependency on technologies they don’t understand (31%).

227.19.1.2 The New Competitive Dynamics

AI creates a peculiar competitive landscape for entrepreneurs. On one hand, it levels the playing field by democratizing access to sophisticated capabilities. A solo entrepreneur with AI tools can compete with established firms in areas like content creation, customer service, and even software development. On the other hand, AI creates new forms of scale advantages. Firms with more data can build better AI systems, and those with better AI systems can acquire more customers and data.

This has led to what researchers term “algorithmic entrepreneurship”, ventures built around proprietary AI systems or unique applications of existing AI. These businesses have different economics than traditional startups: high initial development costs but near-zero marginal costs, winner-take-all dynamics in narrow niches, and value that derives from data and algorithms rather than human capital or physical assets.

The implications for entrepreneurship education and policy are significant. Traditional entrepreneurship programs focusing on business planning and financial modeling become less relevant when AI can generate these in seconds. Instead, successful entrepreneurs need to understand AI capabilities and limitations, identify opportunities for human-AI collaboration, and build organizations that can continuously adapt to rapidly evolving AI technologies. Policymakers face the challenge of supporting AI entrepreneurship while preventing algorithmic monopolies and ensuring that AI’s benefits extend beyond a technical elite.

227.19.2 Field-Experimental Evidence: AI Advice Is Not Self-Implementing

The evidence in this part has so far come from systematic reviews, surveys, and observational funding data, which is the norm in entrepreneurship research and also its central weakness: entrepreneurs who adopt AI differ from those who do not in exactly the ways that also predict growth. The literature’s first completed randomized field experiment, the Kenyan study of Otis et al. (2026) introduced in Section 227.4.1.2, therefore carries weight well beyond its setting, and its design details repay attention.

The researchers recruited 640 owners of small businesses, spanning fast food restaurants, poultry farms, and internet cafes, among others, and randomized access to a GPT-4 powered business mentor delivered over WhatsApp, the channel already used by roughly 90% of Kenyans, against a control condition receiving a standard small-business guide. The mentor was customized for the Kenyan business environment, and its replies paired each recommendation with implementation guidance. Over five months the team collected more than 4,000 firm-outcome observations along with the text of thousands of mentor conversations, so the study can link what was asked, what was advised, and what subsequently happened to revenues and profits at the level of the individual firm.

The pattern of use is where the entrepreneurship-specific insight lives. Entrepreneurs did not treat the mentor as a novelty; they brought it real decisions, a restaurant owner deliberating a menu change, a milk seller weighing product expansion. But what they brought depended on the state of the business. Owners of growing firms asked bounded operational questions about marketing, pricing, and products, the kind of question for which a concrete, implementable answer exists. Owners of struggling firms asked the mentor to solve survival: drought, severe competition, missing working capital. The advice itself was of comparable quality across the two groups, and the divergence in outcomes, positive for the first group and negative for the second, traces to what recipients could implement rather than to what the model said (Otis et al. 2026). Advice that assumes organizational slack, spend a little on promotion, test a new product line, can misfire in a firm that has none.

Reading the result against the older business-training literature sharpens it. Decades of randomized trials of classroom-style management training for small firms in developing countries find average profit effects that are modest, frequently in the range of 5 to 10 percent, and often statistically insignificant, while intensive one-on-one consulting performs better at a cost several orders of magnitude higher per firm (McKenzie 2021). An AI mentor occupies a previously empty point on that cost-effectiveness frontier: individualized like consulting, cheap like a pamphlet, and available at midnight when the actual decision is being made. Seen this way, the Kenya findings are simultaneously encouraging and disciplining. For entrepreneurs able to act on advice, a nearly free intervention produced double-digit percentage gains, an effect size the training literature would consider remarkable. For those who could not, access left them worse off than the control group with its static guide.

Three design implications follow. For distribution, pairing AI advice with the complementary resources that make advice executable, working capital, basic bookkeeping capacity, peer implementation groups, is not an add-on but the mechanism through which the treatment works; the authors themselves point to expanded access to complementary skills and financial resources as the path to broader gains. For product design, a business advisor should diagnose implementability before prescribing: a recommendation that is correct in general can be harmful in the particular when the firm cannot afford the working capital it presumes. And for the democratization narrative that opened this part, the experiment replaces an assumption with a finding: access to elite-grade advice is now nearly free, and access was never the binding constraint for the firms most in need of help. The same logic scales up from firms to countries, as Section 227.20.1 discusses.

227.20 The Global AI Divide

227.20.1 AI and International Development

The global implications of AI for development and inequality represent perhaps the most consequential and least understood aspects of the AI revolution. Korinek and Stiglitz analyzes how AI may simultaneously be labor-saving and resource-saving, fundamentally altering patterns of comparative advantage that have shaped global development for decades. Countries that built development strategies on low-wage manufacturing may find their competitive advantage eroded as AI-enabled automation makes labor costs irrelevant.

Cerutti et al. (2025) present model-based scenarios for AI adoption across countries, revealing a troubling divergence. Under optimistic scenarios where AI capabilities diffuse rapidly, developing countries could leapfrog stages of development, using AI to provide education, healthcare, and financial services without building traditional infrastructure. Under pessimistic scenarios where AI remains concentrated in wealthy nations, the development gap could widen dramatically, with poor countries unable to compete in either manufacturing (lost to AI automation) or services (dominated by AI from rich countries).

The Kenya experiment of Section 227.19.2 functions as a micro-scale test of these scenarios, and its verdict is sobering for the leapfrogging hypothesis in its simplest form. Frontier-model access was delivered over infrastructure the country already had, at essentially zero marginal cost, in exactly the kind of setting where the optimistic scenario predicts the largest returns, and it still produced gains only for the entrepreneurs who already had the capacity to implement advice (Otis et al. 2026). Diffusion of access, the quantity the optimistic scenario treats as the bottleneck, turned out to be the easy part. The complementary skills, working capital, and stable operating environment that convert advice into profits remained scarce, and without them access widened within-country dispersion rather than narrowing it.

227.20.1.1 The New Comparative Advantage

Skare and colleagues conduct a comprehensive empirical exploration linking AI indicators to wealth inequality across countries. They find that AI adoption is associated with reduced within-country inequality in developed nations (as AI helps lower-skilled workers) but increased between-country inequality (as AI-capable nations pull ahead). This suggests that AI might reduce inequality within the global elite while widening the gap between rich and poor nations.

Traditional development economics assumed that countries would progress through stages, agriculture, manufacturing, services, with each stage providing employment for workers displaced from the previous one. AI disrupts this progression. Manufacturing may never provide mass employment in developing countries if AI-powered robots are cheaper than even the lowest-wage workers. Service sectors may be dominated by AI systems operated from anywhere in the world. This leaves developing countries searching for new development models that don’t rely on traditional patterns of structural transformation.

227.20.1.2 Infrastructure and Governance Gaps

the Brookings Institution provide case-based analysis of AI for development, highlighting both opportunities and challenges. On the opportunity side, AI can address critical development challenges: predicting crop yields to improve food security, diagnosing diseases where doctors are scarce, providing personalized education in multiple languages, and enabling financial inclusion through algorithmic credit scoring.

However, realizing these benefits requires overcoming substantial barriers. Infrastructure gaps, unreliable electricity, limited internet connectivity, lack of computational resources, prevent AI deployment in many developing regions. Governance gaps, weak regulatory frameworks, limited technical expertise in government, corruption, mean that AI might be deployed in ways that harm rather than help development. Skills gaps, low digital literacy, limited AI expertise, brain drain of technical talent, prevent developing countries from building indigenous AI capabilities.

Pitt and colleagues propose a factor-based AI approach for developing economies, arguing that development strategies should focus on leveraging abundant factors (young populations eager to learn, unique cultural knowledge, biodiversity data) while working around scarce factors (computational infrastructure, technical expertise, venture capital). They present case studies of successful AI initiatives in developing countries: Rwanda’s drone delivery network for medical supplies, Kenya’s mobile money ecosystem enhanced by AI fraud detection, and India’s Aadhaar biometric identification system enabling AI-powered service delivery.

227.20.1.3 The WTO’s Warning

The World Trade Organization’s 2025 analysis provides a sobering assessment of AI’s impact on global trade and development. AI could boost global trade by reducing transaction costs, improving logistics, and enabling new forms of digital services. However, the benefits will likely concentrate in countries with advanced AI capabilities, potentially reversing decades of progress in integrating developing countries into global value chains.

The report identifies several mechanisms through which AI could widen global inequality. First, AI-powered automation reduces the importance of labor cost advantages, undermining the traditional development path through export-oriented manufacturing. Second, data and computational resources exhibit economies of scale that favor large, wealthy countries. Third, AI systems trained primarily on data from developed countries may not work well in different cultural and economic contexts. Fourth, the complexity of AI systems makes technology transfer more difficult than with previous technologies.

227.21 Conclusion: Navigating the Great Transformation

227.21.1 The Emerging Synthesis

As we synthesize the research findings, several meta-patterns emerge:

227.21.1.1 The Paradox of Progress

AI presents us with multiple paradoxes:

  • It makes individuals more creative while reducing collective creativity
  • It reduces inequality in performance while potentially increasing inequality in employment
  • It augments human capabilities while potentially replacing human workers
  • It democratizes access to expertise while concentrating rewards among fewer people

These paradoxes cannot be resolved through technology alone, they require thoughtful policy responses and social adaptation.

227.21.1.2 The Velocity of Change

The speed of AI adoption and impact exceeds that of previous technological revolutions. Where past transformations unfolded over decades, AI is restructuring work in years. This velocity creates both opportunities and risks:

Opportunities:

  • Rapid productivity gains
  • Quick skill leveling
  • Fast innovation cycles
  • Immediate accessibility

Risks:

  • Insufficient adaptation time
  • Skill obsolescence
  • Social disruption
  • Regulatory lag

227.21.1.3 The Imperative of Agency

Perhaps the most important finding across all studies is that outcomes are not predetermined. The impact of AI depends on choices made by individuals, organizations, and societies:

  • Individual choices about skill development and AI use
  • Organizational choices about implementation and worker support
  • Societal choices about regulation, education, and social support

227.21.2 The Path Forward

The research suggests several principles for navigating the AI transformation:

227.21.2.1 Embrace Augmentation, Prepare for Automation

While focusing on how AI can augment human capabilities, we must also prepare for scenarios where it replaces human work entirely in certain domains.

227.21.2.2 Invest in Continuous Learning

The half-life of skills is shrinking. Educational systems, organizations, and individuals must shift from front-loaded education to continuous learning models.

227.21.2.3 Design for Human Flourishing

As AI handles routine work, we have an opportunity to redesign work around distinctly human capabilities, creativity, empathy, ethical reasoning, and meaning-making.

227.21.2.4 Address Inequality Proactively

The research clearly shows that AI’s benefits are unevenly distributed. Without intervention, AI could exacerbate existing inequalities.

227.21.2.5 Maintain Human Agency

As AI becomes more capable, maintaining human agency and decision-making authority becomes crucial for both practical and ethical reasons.

227.21.3 Final Reflections

The story of AI’s impact on work and society is still being written. The research examined in this chapter represents only the first chapters of what will likely be a multi-decade transformation. What’s clear is that we stand at an inflection point comparable to the Industrial Revolution or the advent of electricity.

The difference this time is that we have the tools, research, data, and analytical frameworks, to understand the transformation as it unfolds. The studies reviewed here provide not just documentation of change but guidance for shaping it. They show us that the future of work in the AI age is not a fixed destination but a landscape of possibilities that we can influence through our collective choices.

As we continue to generate evidence about AI’s impacts, several things remain certain:

  • The transformation will be uneven across sectors, occupations, and individuals
  • Both tremendous opportunities and significant risks lie ahead
  • Human judgment, creativity, and values will remain essential
  • Our responses to AI will shape society for generations

The great transformation is not something happening to us, it’s something we’re actively creating through millions of daily decisions about how to develop, deploy, and live with artificial intelligence. The research shows us the patterns, but we must write the ending.

# The Economics of Large Language Models: An Overview {#sec-llm-economics-overview}

::: {.chapter-subtitle}
How generative AI is reshaping work, creativity, productivity, and markets
:::

Large language models (LLMs) are the first information technology in decades that economists have been able to study almost in real time, from the moment of mass adoption. This chapter surveys what the first wave of rigorous empirical and theoretical research tells us about the economic consequences of generative AI: how it changes individual productivity and collective diversity, how it reshapes labor demand, who adopts it and how intensively, and how it alters the economics of prediction, data, and platforms. The goal is an integrated reference. We first build the conceptual and mathematical scaffolding that organizes the evidence, then review the empirical findings domain by domain, and finally return to the theory to interpret the long-run questions that remain open.

A persistent theme is that the same technology produces opposite-signed effects at different levels of analysis. Generative AI tends to raise the average quality of individual output while compressing its variance, to lift the productivity of lower-skilled workers more than higher-skilled ones where tasks are structured and to reverse that gradient where they are not, and to expand what a single person can produce while narrowing what a population of people collectively explores. Holding these tensions together, rather than collapsing them into a single optimistic or pessimistic story, is the central analytical task of the chapter.

## Conceptual Foundations {#sec-conceptual-foundations}

Before reviewing evidence, we fix definitions and the small amount of formal machinery that makes the empirical results legible. The economics of AI is, at its core, a relabeling of classical questions in the economics of technology, so the right starting point is the vocabulary that labor and innovation economists already use.

### Generative AI as a general-purpose technology {#sec-gpt-definition}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Definition (general-purpose technology).** A *general-purpose technology* (GPT) is a technology that is pervasive across sectors, improves rapidly over time, and spawns complementary innovations in the sectors that adopt it. Steam power, electricity, and the integrated circuit are the canonical examples.
:::

Generative AI fits this definition on all three counts. It is pervasive, because text and code are inputs to almost every occupation. It improves rapidly, because capability scales with compute and data along empirically regular curves. And it is innovation-spawning, because adopting it forces firms to redesign workflows, which is where most of the eventual value is realized. The GPT framing matters for one practical reason: GPTs historically deliver their measured productivity gains only after a lag, once organizations rebuild processes around them. This is the standard explanation for the "productivity paradox" we revisit in @sec-productivity-paradox, and it cautions against reading early aggregate statistics as the ceiling of AI's impact.

### The task-based view of work {#sec-task-based-foundations}

The most useful lens for AI and labor is the *task-based* model developed by @autor2003skill and formalized by @acemoglu2018race and @acemoglu2019automation. An occupation is not an atom; it is a bundle of tasks, and technology acts on tasks, not on job titles. This is why AI can transform an occupation, reweighting which tasks dominate, without eliminating it.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Definition (task-based production).** Output $Y$ is produced by combining a continuum of tasks indexed by $i \in [0,1]$. Each task can be performed by labor or by capital (here, AI). Let $N$ denote labor and $K$ denote AI capital. Aggregate output takes the constant-returns form
$$
Y \;=\; B \exp\!\left( \int_0^1 \ln y(i)\, di \right), \qquad
y(i) \;=\; \alpha_K(i)\, k(i) \;+\; \alpha_L(i)\, \ell(i),
$$
where $y(i)$ is the quantity of task $i$, and $\alpha_K(i), \alpha_L(i)$ are the productivities of AI and labor at that task.
:::

A task is *automated* when AI becomes weakly more cost-effective than labor at performing it, that is, when
$$
\frac{\alpha_K(i)}{R} \;\ge\; \frac{\alpha_L(i)}{W},
$$
where $R$ is the rental cost of AI capital (compute, licensing, integration) and $W$ is the wage. Define the *automation frontier* $I^*$ as the threshold task such that all tasks $i < I^*$ are performed by AI and all tasks $i \ge I^*$ remain with labor. As AI improves, $\alpha_K(i)$ rises and the frontier $I^*$ moves right, displacing labor from newly automated tasks. Korinek and Suh call the moving boundary the *complexity frontier* [@korinek2024scenarios]; it is the same object viewed from the perspective of task difficulty.

This model yields three results that recur throughout the empirical literature.

1. **Comparative advantage, not absolute advantage, determines who keeps a task.** A worker does not need to beat AI at a task in absolute terms to retain it. Labor keeps the tasks where its *relative* productivity $\alpha_L(i)/\alpha_K(i)$ is highest. This is why even highly capable AI leaves substantial work for humans: people reallocate toward the tasks where the gap is smallest.

2. **Displacement and reinstatement are distinct forces.** Automation of tasks below $I^*$ is a *displacement effect* that reduces labor demand. But the same productivity gains, plus capital accumulation, can create new tasks above the old frontier, a *reinstatement effect* that raises labor demand. @acemoglu2019automation show that wages and the labor share rise or fall depending on which force dominates. The "race" in @sec-race-theory is precisely the race between these two.

3. **Wage effects are heterogeneous within occupations.** Because workers hold different task portfolios, reweighting tasks creates winners and losers inside the same job title, exactly the pattern @freund2025job document empirically (@sec-task-recomposition).

### A worked example: automation, augmentation, and net labor demand {#sec-worked-example}

The model is easier to trust once instantiated with numbers. Consider an occupation made of three equally weighted task groups: routine information processing (R), analysis and judgment (A), and client interaction (C). A worker's value added per unit time on each group, before AI, is $\alpha_L = (10, 10, 10)$. Suppose AI raises effective productivity on the tasks the worker still performs (augmentation) but also takes over a share of routine tasks outright (automation).

Concretely, let AI automate 70% of the routine group and augment the worker on the remainder, multiplying human productivity by $1.5$ on routine, $1.4$ on analysis, and $1.1$ on interaction. Per unit of the worker's time, human-performed output becomes
$$
\underbrace{(1-0.7)\cdot 10 \cdot 1.5}_{\text{routine}=4.5} \;+\; \underbrace{10\cdot 1.4}_{\text{analysis}=14} \;+\; \underbrace{10\cdot 1.1}_{\text{interaction}=11} \;=\; 29.5,
$$
versus $30$ before AI. The worker's *output per hour* on retained tasks is essentially unchanged, but the *composition* has shifted decisively away from routine work toward analysis and interaction. Whether headcount rises or falls now depends on demand elasticity. If the cheaper, faster service expands the market enough, the firm hires more of these workers (reinstatement dominates); if demand is inelastic, the same output needs fewer workers (displacement dominates). This single example reproduces, in miniature, why the empirical labor-market findings in @sec-labor-transformation are mixed and context-dependent rather than uniformly negative: the sign of the employment effect is not a property of the technology alone but of the technology interacted with demand.

### Automation versus augmentation {#sec-automation-augmentation-defs}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Definition (automation vs augmentation).** AI *automates* a task when it performs the task in place of a human (capital substitutes for labor at that task). AI *augments* a worker when it raises the worker's productivity at a task the worker still performs (capital complements labor). The same tool can do both, on different tasks, within the same job.
:::

The distinction is not merely descriptive: it predicts the sign of the employment effect. Augmentation raises the marginal product of labor and tends to support or increase employment and wages; automation lowers labor demand for the affected tasks. The empirical regularity that AI helps lower-skilled workers most (@sec-heterogeneity) follows naturally, since novices spend a larger share of time on exactly the routine tasks where AI augmentation is largest and the quality gap to experts is widest.

### AI as a reduction in the cost of prediction {#sec-prediction-cost}

A complementary framing, due to Agrawal, Gans, and Goldfarb, treats machine learning as a sharp drop in the *cost of prediction*. When the price of a fundamental input falls, three things happen: we use more of it, we use more of its complements, and we substitute away from things it replaces. The complements to cheap prediction are *data* (the input) and *judgment* (deciding what to predict and what to do with the prediction). This reframes many business problems as prediction problems: inventory management becomes demand prediction, lending becomes default prediction, and recruiting becomes performance prediction. The policy and organizational implications, including the unbundling of prediction from judgment, are developed in @sec-prediction-economics, and the policy reconsideration this forces is surveyed by @agrawal2019economic.

LLMs extend this logic from numeric prediction to prediction over language and code, which is why their reach is so broad: almost every knowledge task contains a next-token-prediction subproblem somewhere inside it.

### Why individual gains and collective losses coexist {#sec-social-dilemma-foundations}

A formal point unifies the creativity and adoption results. Generative models sample from a learned distribution over human artifacts. Each user, optimizing privately, is drawn toward high-probability regions of that distribution, because high-probability outputs are, on average, higher quality. Privately this is rational and welfare-improving. Collectively, if many users draw from the *same* distribution, the population of outputs concentrates: average quality rises while diversity falls. This is a textbook *social dilemma*, individually optimal choices producing a collectively suboptimal outcome, and it is the through-line connecting the homogenization of writing (@sec-homogenization), the narrowing of scientific focus, and the convergence of advertising creative (@sec-advertising-consumer). The mitigation, in every case, is the same: deliberately price or reward divergence from the statistical center.

With this scaffolding in place, the empirical sections below can be read as measurements of the quantities the model names: the speed at which the automation frontier $I^*$ advances, the size of the augmentation multipliers, the elasticity of demand that converts productivity into employment, and the magnitude of the diversity loss.

## The Dawn of a New Economic Era {#sec-introduction}

In November 2022, a seemingly simple chatbot named ChatGPT was released to the public. Within five days, it had attracted a million users. Within two months, it reached 100 million. By July 2025, approximately 10% of the world's adult population, nearly 800 million people, had become active users [@chatterji2025people]. This explosive adoption represents not just another technology trend, but potentially the most rapid technological transformation in human history.

The speed of this transformation dwarfs previous technological revolutions. Where the personal computer took decades to reshape the workplace, and the internet required years of infrastructure development before achieving mainstream adoption, generative artificial intelligence has infiltrated offices, creative studios, and production floors with unprecedented velocity. As @bick2026rapid document, work adoption of generative AI has matched the pace of personal computer adoption, while overall adoption has exceeded both PCs and the internet when measured from their first mass-market product launches.

Yet this is not merely a story of rapid adoption. It is a tale of fundamental transformation: one that is simultaneously enhancing human creativity while homogenizing it, dramatically boosting individual productivity while threatening entire categories of work, and creating opportunities for some while closing doors for others. The paradoxes embedded in this transformation demand careful examination, for they will shape not just our economic future, but the very nature of human work and creativity.

This chapter tells that story through the lens of rigorous empirical research, drawing on evidence from millions of workers, hundreds of thousands of firms, and dozens of controlled experiments conducted in the first three years of the generative AI revolution. What emerges is a complex portrait of technological change that defies simple narratives of either utopian enhancement or dystopian replacement.

## The Questions That Matter {#sec-key-questions}

As we stand at this inflection point, several critical questions emerge:

1.  **The Creativity Question**: Does AI enhance human creativity, or does it lead to a troubling convergence of ideas and expressions?

2.  **The Productivity Question**: How much more productive can humans become when augmented by AI, and who captures these gains?

3.  **The Employment Question**: Will AI complement or substitute for human workers, and how will this vary across different types of work?

4.  **The Inequality Question**: Does AI level the playing field by helping lower-skilled workers catch up, or does it create new forms of digital divides?

5.  **The Adoption Question**: Who is using these tools, how intensively, and what determines the pace and pattern of adoption?

This chapter systematically addresses each of these questions, building a picture of AI's multifaceted impact on the modern economy.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### The Creativity Paradox {#sec-creativity-paradox}

#### The Dual Nature of AI-Enhanced Creativity {#sec-dual-nature}

The impact of generative AI on human creativity presents us with our first paradox. In a carefully controlled experiment, @doshi2024generative asked writers to craft short stories, with some receiving AI-generated ideas as inspiration. The results were striking: stories written with AI assistance were judged to be more creative, better written, and more enjoyable to read. The effect was particularly pronounced for writers who scored lower on baseline creativity measures, AI appeared to be democratizing creative excellence.

But there was a catch. When the researchers analyzed the similarity between stories, they discovered something troubling: AI-assisted stories were significantly more similar to each other than stories written by humans alone. The technology that made individual writers more creative was simultaneously making collective creativity more homogeneous.

This finding illuminates a fundamental tension in the age of AI. As @doshi2024generative frame it, we face a social dilemma: writers are individually better off using AI, but collectively, society produces a narrower scope of novel content. It's as if AI provides everyone with a more powerful creative engine, but all the engines are manufactured in the same factory, running on the same fuel, producing variations on the same underlying patterns.

#### The Homogenization Effect: A Deeper Look {#sec-homogenization}

To understand why this homogenization occurs, we must consider how generative AI works. These systems are trained on vast corpora of existing human creative works, learning patterns, styles, and structures that appear most frequently in their training data. When humans use AI for creative assistance, they're essentially tapping into a statistical distillation of past human creativity. The AI suggests ideas that are, by design, probable given what has come before.

This creates what we might call a "creative gravity well", AI suggestions pull human creators toward the center of the distribution of existing ideas rather than pushing them toward the edges, where true innovation occurs. The most creative individuals, who might naturally gravitate toward unusual or unprecedented ideas, find themselves gently guided back toward the mainstream. Meanwhile, less naturally creative individuals are lifted up toward this same center point, improving their individual output but contributing to an overall convergence (Figure @fig-creative-convergence-ai-assistance).

This is no longer just a plausible mechanism inferred from one creative-writing study. @jiang2025hivemind (NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper) name the effect the **Artificial Hivemind** and measure it directly at scale, independent of any specific creative task. They build Infinity-Chat, a benchmark of 26,000 real-world, open-ended queries that by construction admit many equally valid answers (no single ground truth), together with 31,250 human judgments (25 independent annotations per example) to establish what a healthy spread of good answers actually looks like. Two distinct failure modes emerge. *Intra-model repetition*: a single model asked the same open-ended question multiple times (at typical sampling temperatures) returns answers that cluster far more tightly than the space of genuinely good answers would allow, the model's own generations pull toward the center of its own distribution. *Inter-model homogeneity*: different model families, trained by different labs on different data, nonetheless converge toward strikingly similar answers to the same open-ended prompt, a pattern the single-model, single-lab framing of the "creative gravity well" cannot fully explain. Both failure modes point to the same underlying force: likelihood-maximizing training (pretraining, then instruction tuning and RLHF, which further sharpens a model toward whatever raters found most acceptable) systematically discounts a *correct but unusual* answer relative to a *typical* one, and does so in a training-data-driven way that different labs, using overlapping web-scale corpora and similar alignment recipes, end up reproducing in common. The economic reading is direct: as AI-assisted output captures a larger share of the visible text, image, and code that future models and future human creators draw on, the "gravity well" is not merely a per-writer effect but a compounding, population-level one, each generation of tools trained partly on the last generation's homogenized output has a narrower distribution to pull toward.
